evidence: factory.py:89 computes dialect = sqlglot_dialect_for_url(cfg.database.url); the same value goes to ReadOnlyGuardRunner (l.91) and RlsGuardRunner (l.98). RlsGuardRunner stores self._dialect (safety/__init__.py:160) and passes it to _refuse_denied_functions -> assert_no_denied_functions(sql, dialect=dialect) (l.196, 206). readonly.py:67-78 returns only keys of _CATALOGS_BY_DIALECT (postgres, mysql, sqlite, l.90-92) or None. _SIDE_EFFECT_FUNCS has keys sqlite, postgres, mysql (l.279, 280, 394), so _DENIED_BY_DIALECT (l.423-426) contains them and _denied_funcs (l.447) selects the per-dialect set. These names are valid sqlglot dialects, so Dialect.get_or_raise (l.542) resolves them. The rejection line concerns an unrelated test and does not apply.

RunSqlTool.execute (run_sql.py:59-61, 182-197) wraps sql_runner.run_sql in try/except Exception and returns ToolResult(success=False, error=str(e), metadata error_type sql_error) with the message intact; it does not inspect exception type, origin or message prefix, so UnsafeSqlError from RlsGuardRunner (safety/__init__.py:196, 203-218, raised as UnsafeSqlError('refusing to execute SQL: ...')) is handled identically to ReadOnlyGuardRunner's. In query_database_impl_with_widgets, the 'except UnsafeSqlError' branch (query_database.py:497-504) matches by type only and re-raises RuntimeError(str(e)); it is defensive since RunSqlTool already converts it. The rejection line concerns a different subject (test column choice) and does not cover this claim.

NORMALIZED (wording-only): The claim does not match the code. assert_no_denied_functions (readonly.py:565-579) calls _parse_statements (readonly.py:536-551). That function refuses empty SQL, an unresolved dialect, the _mysql_parse_sql refusals (backslash-escaped quotes at :493, executable comments at :506, ambiguous double dash at :517) and parse/token errors. apply_rls parses with a bare sqlglot.parse (rls.py:224) and never calls _mysql_parse_sql. A MySQL statement such as SELECT 'it\'s' FROM t with no denylisted function is therefore accepted by apply_rls but refused by _refuse_denied_functions (safety/__init__.py:196, 203-218). That contradicts the claim's 'only denylist or unacceptable-to-_parse_statements' wording as applied to the apply_rls-accepted set. A PostgreSQL data-modifying CTE with no denylisted function is not refused by this step, as the claim says. No source requires the claimed property. The docstring at readonly.py:565-573 states that this check fails closed on _mysql_parse_sql ambiguity. docs/external/row-level-security.md:134 says refusal applies when 'SQL Lens cannot check it for such calls', even with read_only false. This is documented fail-closed behavior, not a defect, and no unchanged file requires otherwise. The rejection line covers a different subject (a routine-lookup test) and does not apply.

readonly.py:575-579: loop over _parse_statements raises UnsafeSqlError('empty parse tree') on a None entry. _parse_statements (536-551) raises on empty/whitespace SQL, unresolvable dialect, parse/tokenize errors; _mysql_parse_sql raises UnsafeSqlError on ambiguity (inside the same try). The docstring (565-573) lists exactly these. For comment-only '-- c' and ';': sqlglot Parser._parse (installed sqlglot parser.py:2313-2337) starts with chunks=[[]] and only appends chunks after a non-final semicolon, so there is always at least one chunk; _parse_batch_statements (2281-2311) appends parse_method(self) per chunk, which returns None for an empty chunk, so the result is [None] and the function raises. An empty list therefore does not arise from sqlglot.parse; if it did, the for loop would be a no-op (no statement to contain a denied function), a defined behavior. Checked against installed sqlglot version only, not the full >=25,<31 range, but the chunks=[[]] structure is long-standing. Rejection line concerns an unrelated test, not applicable. Did not run code.

Compared base readonly.py:536-609 with head readonly.py:536-635. Head _parse_statements (536-551) is the base prologue moved verbatim: same empty-SQL check/message, same Dialect.get_or_raise ValueError -> 'could not resolve SQL dialect: ...', same MySQL/generic-Dialect _mysql_parse_sql call with identical mysql_line_comments arg, same ParseError/TokenError -> 'could not parse SQL: ...'. Head _refuse_denied_function (554-562) is the base isinstance(exp.Func) / _func_name_candidates & denied_funcs / sorted(offending)[0] block with identical message, called per node at 635 inside the same walk after the DML/DDL and SELECT INTO checks. assert_select_only's remaining statement-count, empty-tree, SHOW, root-type, _denied_funcs(dialect) ordering are unchanged. No branch, exception type or message changed. The new assert_no_denied_functions is additive and not part of the claim.

Both functions obtain statements via the shared _parse_statements (readonly.py:536-551), which raises UnsafeSqlError for empty SQL (538-539), unresolvable dialect (542-544), _mysql_parse_sql ambiguity (547-548), and ParseError/TokenError (550-551). The multi-statement hint input (SELECT 1; SELECT pg_sleep(1)) is not among the listed inputs; assert_select_only refuses by count (590-593) while the denylist function walks every statement and refuses pg_sleep, so it still fails closed on the denied call. factory.py:97-98 wraps in RlsGuardRunner only `if cfg.rls:`; it is the only construction site in src (grep). So with no rules the runner is absent and ReadOnlyGuardRunner (gated on read_only at factory.py:90) is unchanged. Even if constructed with empty rules, safety/__init__.py:195-196 calls _refuse_denied_functions only `if self._rules:`, and line 197 sets require_base_tables only when rules exist or the caller passed it. factory.py:88-98 wraps RowCapRunner, then ReadOnlyGuardRunner (if read_only), then RlsGuardRunner (if cfg.rls) last, so RLS is outermost. RlsGuardRunner.run_sql (safety/__init__.py:162-200) rewrites, calls _refuse_denied_functions -> assert_no_denied_functions (line 195-196, 206) when rules exist, and only then calls self._inner.run_sql (line 198), which is the ReadOnlyGuardRunner when read_only is true. So the denylist check runs ahead of the read-only guard's own copy, as docs line 204 states. The rejection line concerns an unrelated test and does not apply.

relations.py:110-134 verify_base_tables computes `called = _called_names(...) if dialect in ('postgres','mysql') else []` and runs _refuse_database_routines only when called is non-empty, so routine verification holds for PostgreSQL and MySQL and SQLite runs relation checks only. sqlite/sql_runner.py:137-146 calls verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect='sqlite') under require_base_tables, so relations are verified there. The doc sentence at row-level-security.md:204 is unqualified, but the same doc states at line 45 'SQLite has no stored functions and runs neither lookup' and line 47 that SQLite's check is relation-types only; since SQLite has no database-defined routines, nothing is left unverified, and the sentence is consistent with the code. The rejection line about the MySQL fake-catalog test concerns a different subject and was not relied on.

relations.py:180-187 the postgres pg_class query selects c.relkind, n.nspname, c.relname, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid). Row index 3 is read as is_child (line 193). Lines 194-199 raise TypeError when it is not a bool, and verify_base_tables' generic except (137-154) turns that into a sanitized 'could not verify' RlsError, so it is a failed lookup. Lines 200-204 raise RlsError for a child. The check runs per relation in the query and consults no rule or parent name. The rejection line is about a different MySQL routine-test subject and does not cover this claim.

Traced by reading only; I could not execute sqlglot (no run tool), and the rejection line does not cover this claim. In the installed sqlglot parser (.venv/.../sqlglot/parser.py:1953, 5251-5253) SUPPORTS_PARTITION_SELECTION defaults False, and neither dialects/mysql.py nor any dialect overrides it. So for `FROM orders PARTITION (p0)` the PARTITION clause is not parsed as a partition. PARTITION is in ID_VAR_TOKENS (parser.py:823), so _parse_table_alias (parser.py:4415-4445) most likely reads it as the table alias with column list (p0). If so, the exp.Table node for orders is kept and no ParseError is raised, so apply_rls (rls.py:282-297) would inject the predicate. The qualifier would be table.alias_or_name, i.e. `PARTITION`. The regenerated SQL would then probably be `orders AS PARTITION(p0) WHERE PARTITION.<col> = ...`. That is likely invalid MySQL (it fails, not leaks), and it is not the partition selection the doc describes. No test in the repo exercises this input (grep of tests found none for MySQL PARTITION). The claim that the table is seen and not hidden is plausible, but the doc's wording of how it works is unverified. Without running `sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT * FROM orders PARTITION (p0)', dialect='mysql')` and `apply_rls` I cannot settle it. Command not run: that parse plus apply_rls with a rule on orders under dialect mysql.

relations.py:84-107 _called_names tokenizes via sqlglot Dialect(dialect).tokenize, pairs each token with its follower (itertools.pairwise), and keeps tokens followed by L_PAREN that are VAR or IDENTIFIER, or whose upper text is in the dialect tokenizer KEYWORDS (covers IN, AS, DECIMAL, REPLACE). A schema. prefix needs no special handling: the name token immediately before ( is collected either way. Matches the doc claim. The rejection line concerns an unrelated test and does not apply.

No installed sqlglot source was found (globs for sqlglot/expressions.py under the repo and .venv returned nothing; a wider search timed out), so I could not read exp.StrPosition's parse names. The REPLACE half is pinned: tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:597-604 asserts the postgres tokenizer's token for REPLACE is neither VAR nor IDENTIFIER. The strpos half is only indirectly supported: test_rls_views.py:619-629 shows a rewritten strpos call executes under a different name and the lookup excludes 'str_position', but that does not show that strpos parses to StrPosition. Missing evidence: sqlglot's expressions.py for the supported range (>=25.0,<31).

relations.py:237-269 _refuse_database_routines issues a single parameterized cursor.execute per statement. PostgreSQL (248-254): pg_catalog.pg_proc JOIN pg_namespace WHERE nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema') AND (proname = ANY(%s) OR lower(proname) = ANY(%s)); no signature filter, so extension routines and all signatures match. MySQL (257-262): information_schema.ROUTINES WHERE ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' AND LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (%s,...). A matching row raises RlsError naming the function via row[0] (265-269). verify_base_tables (122-134): returns early only when both relations and called names are empty; the routine check runs under `if called:` independent of relations. Minor nuance: the lookup runs only when the statement has a call-position name, which the claim's 'per statement' wording does not spell out. The rejection line concerns a different subject (the unit test's fake catalog) and is not needed for this verdict.

relations.py verify_base_tables wraps everything (_relations/sqlglot parse+tokenize at 123, _called_names at 124, connection.cursor, both lookups, cursor.close) in one try (122-134). `except RlsError: raise` (135) passes refusals through; `except Exception` (137) logs logger.warning(..., exc_info=True) (146-151) and raises RlsError(f"row-level security could not verify {checked}; query blocked") from exc (152-154). checked is 'relation types or function calls' for postgres/mysql and 'relation types' otherwise i.e. SQLite (141-145), matching the doc's two messages. Traced inputs: a 2-tuple row without child flag -> row[3] IndexError (193) is an Exception, caught; non-bool flag -> TypeError raised at 197, caught; lookup that raises or tokenizer TokenError/ParseError -> Exception, caught. Caveat: a non-Exception BaseException (KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, CancelledError) from cursor.execute is not caught and propagates unlogged and unsanitized; it still fails closed (the query does not run) and is not an 'error' in the doc's sense, so I treat the claim as holding for Exception-class errors. The rejection line concerns a MySQL test fake's column choice, unrelated to this claim.

relations.py:98-106 collects only tokens (VAR/IDENTIFIER/keyword) whose next token is L_PAREN, so `o.fn` with no `(` is never collected and the routine check does not see it. PostgreSQL's 'SQL Functions on Composite Types' documents that a function taking a composite (table row) argument can be written as `table.function` attribute notation, equivalent to function(table), with a real column taking precedence; the doc text at row-level-security.md:51 matches this. The rejection line is unrelated to this claim.

docs row-level-security.md:53 says: with rules configured, __init__ looks past RlsGuardRunner, ReadOnlyGuardRunner and RowCapRunner to the first runner beneath, raises TypeError unless its run_sql names a require_base_tables parameter, a bare **kwargs does not qualify, and a custom wrapper is checked as that runner. safety/__init__.py:228 loops only while type(runner) is exactly one of those three wrappers (so subclasses/custom wrappers are checked themselves); :149-155 raises TypeError only if rules and not _declares_relation_check; :243-247 requires a named param of kind KEYWORD_ONLY or POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, so **kwargs (VAR_KEYWORD) does not qualify. The listed checks (view/relation-kind, PG child-table, PG/MySQL routine) match the paragraphs at lines 41-45 and the RlsGuardRunner docstring. The rejection line concerns a test and is unrelated.

safety/__init__.py:195-196 RlsGuardRunner.run_sql calls _refuse_denied_functions(rewritten, dialect) only `if self._rules`; with no rules nothing is run. _refuse_denied_functions (203-218) calls assert_no_denied_functions and wraps/raises UnsafeSqlError (also fail-closed on unexpected exceptions). It is independent of database.read_only (RlsGuardRunner does not consult it). readonly.py:565-579 assert_no_denied_functions uses _denied_funcs(dialect) and _refuse_denied_function per walked node, exactly as assert_select_only does (616, 621-635), and omits the single-statement, root-type, DML/DDL and SELECT INTO checks. Claim matches. The rejection line is about a different subject (routine-lookup test) and was not relied on.

readonly.py:354 lists pg_sleep in the PostgreSQL _SIDE_EFFECT_FUNCS set (inside the postgres dialect entry before line 408); readonly.py:416-429 puts generate_series in _ALWAYS_DENIED_FUNCS, merged into every _DENIED_BY_DIALECT entry and _DENIED_UNION. assert_no_denied_functions (565-579) raises UnsafeSqlError on empty SQL, unresolvable dialect, parse/tokenize error. safety/__init__.py:195-196 calls _refuse_denied_functions whenever self._rules is non-empty, independent of database.read_only; it (203-218) converts UnsafeSqlError and any other exception into a refusal 'refusing to execute SQL'. docs/external/row-level-security.md:133 matches relations.py. verify_base_tables (110-154) refuses PG child tables via pg_inherits (181-204, RlsError), refuses called names matching routines (_refuse_database_routines 237-269), and any lookup exception fails closed with RlsError (137-154). Postgres lookup checks pg_proc outside pg_catalog/information_schema (248-250); MySQL filters information_schema.ROUTINES with ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION' (258-259), so stored procedures are not matched, consistent with the doc saying 'function' and the claim's 'on MySQL covers stored functions'. Absolute-style input considered: a MySQL stored procedure name called in a query; it is not matched, and a procedure cannot be called in an expression, so the doc is not contradicted. The rejection line concerns a unit-test fake and does not affect this doc claim.

relations.py:171-204: for every relation from _relations (traverse_scope over all scopes, so CTE bodies and subqueries are included; unaccounted Table nodes raise at :79-80), the PostgreSQL branch looks up pg_inherits for the resolved relation and raises RlsError at :200-204 when the table is a child. The check reads only the catalog and never consults the RLS rules, so a rule naming orders_2024 does not exempt it. Other relkinds (e.g. foreign tables) fall to the not-a-base-table refusal at :231. Parent queries: a rule on orders is injected as a WHERE on the orders scope, and PostgreSQL's plain `FROM orders` scans child rows, so the predicate filters them. `ONLY orders` is not what the claim describes; it either parses as a table with the predicate applied (children excluded anyway) or fails to parse and fails closed. I did not confirm which of the two happens. Absolute-claim input traced: a rule on orders_2024 plus SELECT * FROM orders_2024, which is refused at :200. The same input inside a CTE is refused too, through scope traversal.

relations.py:180-204 queries pg_inherits with `i.inhrelid = c.oid` for only the referenced relation (to_regclass of the name) and refuses only when that relation is itself a child. A parent that is not itself a child is not refused, even if its child has another parent. So a multi-parent child is reachable through each parent, which matches docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 ('readable through each of them, so give every such parent its own rule'). The rejection line in the item concerns a different subject (MySQL routine test) and was not relied on.

docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 states name-alone matching and call-only checking. Code: _called_names (relations.py:84-107) tokenizes and collects only tokens immediately followed by L_PAREN (whitespace irrelevant, string literals are single tokens so never collected; schema prefix is ignored since only the token before '(' is taken, so pg_catalog.upper( yields 'upper'). _refuse_database_routines (237-269) queries pg_proc in schemas other than pg_catalog/information_schema (or MySQL ROUTINES) by name only, case-insensitive, across schemas and signatures, with no check on which function the call resolves to. Trace: SELECT upper(name) with public.UPPER -> names {upper}; lower(proname)=ANY matches -> RlsError. pg_catalog.upper(...) likewise refused. Docstring at 240-244 agrees. Rejection line concerns a test column-pinning matter, not this claim.

docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 says to grant EXECUTE only on reviewed functions and revoke PostgreSQL's default EXECUTE grant to PUBLIC on the rest. PostgreSQL's Privileges chapter (ddl-priv) lists EXECUTE on functions/procedures as granted to PUBLIC by default for newly created functions. I am relying on my knowledge of that documentation, not a fetched copy. The bullet's advice (REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC) matches that default.

SQLite runner (sqlite/sql_runner.py:137-146) passes require_base_tables into verify_base_tables(conn, sql, dialect='sqlite') inside a BEGIN. In relations.py:124 the routine-name check runs only for postgres/mysql, and the child-table check (pg_inherits) is postgres-only (190-204); SQLite uses _sqlite_kind and refuses views/unverifiable kinds (174-175, 227). SQLite has no table inheritance/partition children and no database-defined stored routines, so the child-table and routine clauses of base.py:30-33 have nothing to refuse there; the narrower scope is consistent with the docstring (the flag is honored, not ignored, as base.py:34 requires). verify_base_tables' own docstring (relations.py:110-121) and the error message (140-145) explicitly state the postgres/mysql scoping. The rejection line concerns a MySQL test fake and does not bear on this claim.

sql_runner.py:168-169 calls verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect="postgres") on the live execution connection before the is_read_shaped/execute path (line 171+). In relations.py verify_base_tables (110-134) opens a cursor on that connection, runs _verify_relations and _refuse_database_routines. The postgres branch of _verify_relations (176-204) selects an EXISTS over pg_catalog.pg_inherits and raises RlsError for child tables (200-204). _refuse_database_routines (246-254) queries pg_catalog.pg_proc outside pg_catalog/information_schema and raises RlsError on a match. The rejection line concerns the MySQL test and is not relevant to this claim.

sql_runner.py:137-138 calls verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect="mysql") on the live pymysql conn, before the is_read_shaped/execute at 140-155. relations.py:122-134: for mysql, _called_names computes call names (line 124), a cursor is taken from the passed connection (127), and _refuse_database_routines runs when names exist (131-132). relations.py:255-262 (mysql else-branch) executes SELECT ROUTINE_NAME FROM information_schema.ROUTINES WHERE ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' AND LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...); a match raises RlsError (264-269). The lookup therefore runs on the same connection before execution. The rejection line about the fake-catalog test concerns test strength, not this claim.

safety/__init__.py:14-21 says the engine runner verifies no called name matches a routine defined in a PostgreSQL or MySQL database, and that any failed catalog lookup blocks the query. relations.py verify_base_tables (110-154) runs _refuse_database_routines only for postgres/mysql (line 124), and _refuse_database_routines (237-269) queries pg_proc outside pg_catalog/information_schema for PostgreSQL and information_schema.ROUTINES for MySQL. The MySQL filter ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' (line 259) leaves out procedures. That is correct because a procedure cannot be called inside a SELECT, and _called_names collects only call-position names. Error paths: an RlsError is re-raised (135-136). Any other exception from a lookup, including a revoked grant or lost connection, is logged and converted to RlsError('could not verify ...; query blocked') at 137-154. A match raises RlsError at 265. The docstring matches the code. The rejection line concerns a test and is not needed for this verdict.

ci.yml:97-101 mysql service sets MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: sqllens and MYSQL_USER/PASSWORD sqllens; the health check uses root/-psqllens. Step at ci.yml:149-150 connects with pymysql to 127.0.0.1 as root/sqllens and runs SET GLOBAL log_bin_trust_function_creators = 1 then closes. SET GLOBAL is not transactional, so it takes effect without a commit (pymysql's default autocommit=False only affects DML). The mysql:8.0 image defaults MYSQL_ROOT_HOST to %, so root can connect over TCP, and root holds the privilege to set the variable. Per MySQL's stored-program binary logging rules, with binary logging on (the 8.0 default) and no SUPER, CREATE FUNCTION is rejected unless this variable is 1. tests/connectors/test_connectors.py:233-250 creates the function through build_sql_runner(mysql_url), and mysql_url is the sqllens user (ci.yml:112), a non-SUPER user. The rejection line (about _FakeCatalog) concerns a different subject and does not affect this claim.

relations.py:122-154: _relations (parse_one, line 62) and _called_names (dialect.tokenize, line 96) are both called inside the try at lines 123-124. `except RlsError: raise` (135-136) re-raises RlsError unchanged, including those raised in _relations at lines 70/80. `except Exception` (137) catches everything else. sqlglot's ParseError and TokenError both derive from SqlglotError(Exception), so they are caught and converted to RlsError at 152-154 (from exc), before any cursor is opened or the query runs. For `SELECT f(1` parse_one raises ParseError. For `SELECT f('unterminated` the tokenizer raises TokenError, either inside parse_one or at line 96 if parse_one did not raise. RlsGuardRunner.run_sql (safety/__init__.py:166-200) computes `rewritten = apply_rls(...)` and passes args.model_copy(update={'sql': rewritten}) to the inner runner with require_base_tables=True when rules exist (line 197). So the checked SQL is the executed rewritten SQL on the same connection. Absolute-input trace: a stacked wrapper order (RowCap/ReadOnly beneath or above RLS) does not alter sql; no wrapper between modifies args.sql after the rewrite. The rejection line concerns a different subject (a test) and does not apply.

relations.py:122-132 computes called names for postgres/mysql only and returns early only if both relations and called are empty; _refuse_database_routines runs whenever called is non-empty, even with no relations. relations.py:180-204 selects EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid) as column 4 (row[3]). pg_inherits holds one row per direct parent link keyed by inhrelid, so every partition, sub-partition and inheritance child at any depth has its own row and EXISTS is true; a top-level table has none. psycopg2's default typecaster maps PostgreSQL boolean to Python bool. Lines 193-199 raise TypeError for any non-bool; verify_base_tables (lines 135-154) catches non-RlsError exceptions, logs, and raises RlsError with the sanitized message 'row-level security could not verify ... ; query blocked'. A sub-partition traces through 192-204 as kind 'r'/'p', is_child True, and is refused. The rejection line concerns the MySQL routine test and is not relevant.

relations.py:188-204 (postgres branch). row[3] is read only at line 193 inside `if kind in _BASE_TABLE_KINDS['postgres']` (= {'r','p'}, line 52). A metadata view (kind 'v' with (nspname, relname) in _METADATA_VIEWS) hits `continue` at line 190-191 before any row[3] read. A non-metadata 'v' or 'm' skips the child check and is refused at 227-230 (_VIEW_KINDS has v, m). 'f' is in neither set and is refused at 231-234 ('could not verify a base table'). A missing row gives kind None (line 189), skips both branches, is not in _VIEW_KINDS, and is refused at 231-234. So non-r/p kinds never need a child flag. The rejection line is about a different subject (MySQL routine lookup test) and does not apply.

relations.py _verify_relations (157-234) has no try/except around cursor.execute/fetchone, so a raising lookup propagates. The non-boolean child flag raises TypeError at 197 (only reachable for base-table kinds); RlsError is a plain Exception subclass (rls.py:70), so TypeError is not RlsError. verify_base_tables calls _verify_relations inside its try (122-130), re-raises only RlsError (135-136), and for other exceptions logs logger.warning(..., exc_info=True) at 146-151 before raising a sanitized RlsError. Docstring matches. The rejection line concerns a different subject and does not apply.

relations.py:247-254 passes (names, names) as a list of str for two `%s` placeholders. The dependency is psycopg2 (pyproject.toml:55 psycopg2-binary>=2.9), which adapts a Python list to ARRAY['a','b'], and string literals in an ARRAY[] resolve to text[]. So `p.proname::text = ANY(ARRAY[...])` and `lower(p.proname::text) = ANY(...)` are valid text = ANY(text[]) comparisons. The schema filter excludes pg_catalog and information_schema. The caller (relations.py:131-132) only calls this when `called` is non-empty, so the empty-list case, which would adapt to '{}' and need a cast, cannot arise. I judged the psycopg2 adaptation from its documented behavior and did not run it against a live database. The rejection line concerns the MySQL fake-cursor test and is not relevant to this claim.

relations.py:255-262 (MySQL arm): SELECT ROUTINE_NAME FROM information_schema.ROUTINES WHERE ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION' AND LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (<', '.join(['%s']*len(names))>) LIMIT 1, params tuple(names); no schema predicate. Caller at line 131-132 only invokes it when `called` is non-empty, so the IN list is never empty. Lines 263-269: only a non-None row raises RlsError; a None row falls through, letting the call through. information_schema.ROUTINES only exposes routines the connected account has privileges on (MySQL documented visibility rule), so invisible routines are not found, as the claim states. The rejections line concerns the test's column choice, not this claim; the verdict rests on the code read directly.

relations.py:246-262: Postgres query selects from pg_catalog.pg_proc joined to pg_namespace with WHERE nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema') and matches only on proname (no argument/signature filter, no other schema filter). tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:519-520 comment says a direct child (orders_2024) and grandchild (orders_2024_q1) are both recorded in pg_inherits whatever their relkind. Per PostgreSQL pg_inherits docs, each inheriting or partition relation (inhrelid = its own oid) has a row for each direct parent, covering both INHERITS and declarative partitioning, and any relkind (r or p). A grandchild or sub-partition has its own row pointing to its immediate parent. So the claim holds. The test parametrizes relkind r/p for the child and uses 'r' for the grandchild, consistent. (2) kind not r/p (e.g. foreign table 'f', None) -> refused by line 231-234: fails closed, not a child. (5) `not relations and not called` early return: only with no relation references, outside the trigger which requires a referenced child. (6) mid-level partitions are also children and are refused, consistent with the claim. No departure found. Not exercised: real-database run.
